title: Another self
hook: Aristotle: a friend is another self (Nicomachean Ethics 9.4)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was philia, Aristotle's word for the love between friends. Your line was friends of the good. Today, he goes a step further, in two Greek words.

Good news arrives, and some people's thumbs go straight to one particular name. Bad news, the same name. Nobody decided that on purpose; it just grew. In the ninth book of his Ethics, Aristotle looks at that kind of bond and asks an odd question: where does it come from? His answer starts somewhere unexpected, not with the friend at all, but with how a good person lives with themself.
screen: `ONE NAME FOR GOOD NEWS.` → `AN ODD QUESTION.`

segments.voice: First, the marks of a friend. Aristotle lists what people take friendship to mean: wishing good to someone for their sake, wishing them to exist and to live, spending time with them, choosing the same things, sharing their griefs and their joys. Second, it starts at home. Then he turns the list around. A good person already relates to themself this way: wants their own good, wants to go on living, is glad of their own company, and isn't at war inside. Third, another self. And so, he says, the good person is to a friend as to themself, for a friend is another self: in Greek, two words, allos autos. Not a copy. Someone whose good matters to you the way your own does, whose griefs land on you as if they were yours. Fourth, the warning inside. He then draws bad people as the opposite: at odds with themselves, running from their own company, full of regret for what they've chosen, with no friendly feeling even toward themselves. Some readers take a hopeful thought from the passage: peace inside and friendship outside may grow from the same root, and tending one may help the other.
screen: `THE MARKS OF A FRIEND.` · `IT STARTS AT HOME.` · `ALLOS AUTOS, ANOTHER SELF.` · `THE WARNING INSIDE.` · then, large: `ANOTHER SELF.`

segments.voice: Bring one friend to mind and, breathing in, wish them what you'd wish yourself today: rest, a good meal, an easy hour, some good news. Breathing out, if it isn't too hard, wish yourself the same, and go back and forth, friend and self, until the two wishes start to sound alike. If one comes easily and the other is hard, just notice which, without judging it.
Another self. Aristotle's phrase, allos autos: a friend is someone whose good matters to you the way your own does. Today's word.
Your line: isn't at war inside. Peace at home, and a friend as another self. Rest well.

howItsDone: Aristotle's idea of the friend as another self, from book nine of the Nicomachean Ethics, is studied in philosophy courses, and some readers use it to reflect on how they treat friends and themselves.

notes: Aristotle paraphrased (no translation on the validator's public-domain list).
List of friendship's marks and the good man's relation to himself follow 9.4 (1166a); 'a friend is another self' (allos autos) at 1166a31–32. Confirm the Greek phrase and pronunciation.
The bad man's division against himself and flight from his own company at 1166b; 'even to themselves' compresses his point; confirm.

Audit: the fourth teach section said Aristotle's warning was about 'people who are at odds with themselves' who 'find it hard to be friends to anyone'. In 9.4 (1166b) he is describing bad (phauloi) people, and says they lack friendly feeling toward themselves; the 'to anyone' was not in the text. Rewritten to attribute the picture to bad people as Aristotle draws them, and the narrator's 'read gently, it's a hopeful thought' now credited to 'some readers'. Match pair adjusted. Carry ('answer as you'd want to be answered') kept; day 825's carry changed so the golden-rule phrasing isn't repeated.
